SCENARIOS.name: Typhoon over Ormoc Bay
SCENARIOS.lead: CDRRMO / EOC (IC designated by the Mayor)
SCENARIOS.blurb: A strong typhoon (exercise name "Bagyong Lunhaw") tracks across Leyte. Storm surge threatens the Ormoc Bay coastline; rain swells the Anilao and Malbasag rivers.
SCENARIOS.context: Ormoc City sits at the head of Ormoc Bay with the city proper between the Anilao and Malbasag rivers. The CDRA rates Naungan, Linao, Punta, Alegria, Batuan and Macabug as high storm-surge risk, with Linao, Tambulilid, Naungan and Ipil the most vulnerable; about 17.65% of the city's area is surge-susceptible. In November 2013 30,546 houses were destroyed (PHP 2.07 billion); Agaton (April 2022) affected 19,262 families in 38 barangays. RA 12287 allows a State of Imminent Disaster when the PDRA shows severe impact, recommended by RDRRMC 8 no later than 3 days before impact.

phases.name: Forecast & PDRA

warn.t: PAGASA: Typhoon outlook · no TCWS yet

situation: PAGASA's outlook shows a typhoon expected to make landfall over Leyte in about 96 hours, intensifying to typhoon category. The forecast cone passes over Ormoc Bay.

Your hazard maps show about 9,000 families in surge- and flood-prone areas (Linao, Naungan, Punta, Alegria, Batuan, Macabug, Ipil, Tambulilid). The CDRRMC can meet this afternoon. Under RA 12287 a State of Imminent Disaster rests on a PDRA showing severe impact, and the IRR works on a 3-day lead time; RDRRMC 8 has 24 hours to answer a city request. You are inside the window now.
phases.intel: Planning: the PDRA template is ready. The AA fund line in this year's LDRRMF has a balance. RDRRMC 8 answers declaration requests within 24 hours, so the request must go out today to keep the 3-day window. NDRRMC operational guidelines on triggers per hazard are still pending.
phases.hint: Which instrument lets the city act before impact, and how long does it need?
phases.discuss: What is our trigger for pre-emptive evacuation, and who signs it?

opts.t: Convene the CDRRMC for a PDRA today; if it shows severe impact, request a State of Imminent Disaster from RDRRMC 8 and prepare AA from the AA fund line. Raise the EOC to Blue.
opts.why: Uses the 3-day window RA 12287 and its IRR work on, and funds early action from the correct source. The PDRA comes first and drives the request.

opts.t: Wait for PAGASA to raise Signal No. 1 before convening anyone; the track may still change.
opts.why: By Signal No. 1 (about 36 h lead time) the 3-day window for a declaration has closed and pre-positioning time is lost.

opts.t: Ask the Sangguniang Panlungsod to declare a state of calamity now so the QRF can buy relief goods.
opts.why: A state of calamity (RA 10121, Sec. 16) responds to a disaster that has occurred. Anticipatory action uses RA 12287 and the AA fund line, not the QRF.

opts.t: Raise the EOC to Blue and send a text blast, but leave the PDRA to the barangays.
opts.why: Alerting is good, but the PDRA is a city-level, multi-office assessment. Without it there is no basis for the declaration or AA.

phases.name: Pre-emptive evacuation

warn.t: TCWS No. 2 · Storm surge warning: 2–3 m

situation: Signal No. 2 is up over Leyte; PAGASA projects Signal No. 4 by tonight and a 2–3 m storm surge along Ormoc Bay. RDRRMC 8 has acted on the request and the Mayor has signed the EO.
Only 1,120 families have moved. Some coastal households in Linao and Naungan say they will stay to guard their homes and boats. Several schools are listed as evacuation centers.
phases.intel: CSWDO: 40 ECs ready, but 12 are in flood-prone schools. 310 families include persons with disability, older persons or pregnant women. PNP can support enforcement if the Mayor orders forced evacuation for the surge zone.
phases.hint: Who recommends forced evacuation, and who comes first?
phases.discuss: How do we move people who refuse, without losing trust?

opts.t: On CDRRMO's recommendation the Mayor orders pre-emptive evacuation now, forced for the surge zone. Move vulnerable families first, skip ECs in flood-prone schools, pre-position food packs and rescue teams at safe staging areas, and designate the IC.
opts.why: Matches RA 10121 (the LDRRMO recommends pre-emptive or forced evacuation) and moves people while roads are open. Prioritizing vulnerable groups and safe ECs avoids a second evacuation.

opts.t: Wait for Signal No. 3 to make the evacuation order stronger.
opts.why: Waiting shortens lead time to about 18 h and pushes evacuation into the night and the rain. The surge warning already justifies action.

opts.t: Leave evacuation to each BDRRMC; the city will just open the ECs.
opts.why: Barangays are first responders, but surge evacuation crosses barangay lines. The city must coordinate transport, ECs and enforcement under one plan.

opts.t: Evacuate everyone citywide to the nearest schools at once.
opts.why: Over-evacuating clogs roads and fills unsafe ECs. Target the exposure your hazard maps show.

phases.name: Landfall
situation: The eye passed north of the city at 01:30H. Winds remain at typhoon strength. Cell sites are down in most of the city and power is out. 54 rescue requests have reached the EOC by radio and runners, mostly from riverside areas along the Anilao.
Two roads to upland barangays are blocked by fallen trees. Rescue teams are asking to deploy now.
phases.intel: SOFR: sustained winds are still above safe limits for boat and line work until about 05:00H. Two radio repeaters are working; the satellite phone at the EOC is working.
phases.hint: Life safety includes responders. What do the winds allow right now?
phases.discuss: How do we sort 54 requests when we cannot reach all of them at once?

opts.t: Hold boat teams at staging until the Safety Officer clears winds; meanwhile triage the 54 requests in the EOC by life threat, assign them to divisions by area, keep radios on the repeaters, and request augmentation through RDRRMC 8.
opts.why: Protects responders, uses the waiting time to prioritize, keeps a workable span of control by area, and asks for help through the proper channel before local capacity runs out.

opts.t: Send every rescue team out now; people are on rooftops.
opts.why: Deploying boats in typhoon winds risks losing the teams you need for the next 72 hours. The Safety Officer has authority to stop this.

opts.t: Wait for daylight and full communications before doing anything.
opts.why: Responders should wait for safe winds, not for perfect conditions. The EOC can triage, plan and request support now.

opts.t: Let each barangay captain call AFP and PCG directly for help.
opts.why: Direct calls bypass the EOC and break unity of command. Augmentation is requested and tracked through the EOC and RDRRMC 8.

phases.name: Assessment & transition
situation: All signals are lifted. Rescue is nearly complete. 6,450 families remain in ECs, including 12 schools that DepEd wants back for classes.
Partial damage reports show houses and farms destroyed in coastal and upland barangays. The State of Imminent Disaster has been lifted. Media are asking for the death toll.
phases.intel: Planning: RDANA teams are ready. The CDRRMC meets at 13:00H. Finance notes that the AA report to OCD is due within 45 days of the lifting of the declaration.
phases.hint: Which assessment justifies the next declaration, and what report is now running on a clock?
phases.discuss: What criteria tell us response is over and recovery can start?

opts.t: Deploy RDANA teams; on their findings the CDRRMC recommends a state of calamity to the Sangguniang Panlungsod. Plan the move from school ECs, start the 45-day AA report, release only verified casualty figures, and set a demobilization plan and AAR date.
opts.why: Evidence first (RDANA), the correct body for the declaration, the RA 12287 reporting clock, verified public information, and an orderly demobilization.

opts.t: Release the barangays' early estimate of the death toll so media stop calling.
opts.why: Unverified casualty figures cause distress and must be corrected later. The PIO releases figures verified through Planning and the MDM process.

opts.t: Close all ECs today so classes can resume tomorrow.
opts.why: Families with destroyed houses have nowhere to go. Transition needs alternative shelter, not a deadline.

opts.t: Declare a state of calamity by Mayor's EO today, before RDANA.
opts.why: Under RA 10121, Sec. 16 the Sanggunian declares on the CDRRMC's recommendation; RDANA gives the basis.

SCENARIOS.name: Anilao–Malbasag flash flood
SCENARIOS.lead: CDRRMO (IC) with BDRRMCs, BFP and PNP
SCENARIOS.blurb: Intense rain over the upper watershed sends a flash flood down the Anilao and Malbasag rivers into the city proper at night. Lead time: about three hours.
SCENARIOS.context: On 5 November 1991 Tropical Storm Thelma (Uring) sent floodwaters down the Anilao and Malbasag rivers into the city proper; the former District 26 (Isla Verde), now part of Barangay West, was among the hardest hit and thousands died. The Ten-Year Plan counts 46 barangays with critical flood risk (59,545 people), and the CDRA rates 35 barangays as flooding every 1–3 years. Flash floods give hours, not days: below RA 12287's 3-day window, so early action rests on the city's own discretion and contingency plan, which the IRR expressly allows.

phases.name: Early warning
situation: PAGASA has raised an Orange rainfall warning (15–30 mm per hour) over western Leyte. The upstream rain gauge reads 48 mm in the last hour; the river gauge at the Anilao bridge is rising fast.
Your flood model gives about three hours before water overtops the banks in West, East and South. About 3,800 riverside families are exposed.
phases.intel: Planning: the upstream gauge has exceeded the alarm threshold in the community early warning system. A State of Imminent Disaster under RA 12287 is built around a 3-day lead time, so it does not fit here. The IRR (Rule IV, Sec. 1) still lets LGUs take anticipatory action at their own discretion, and RA 10121 and the contingency plan apply.
phases.hint: Three hours. Which law fits, and what has to move first?
phases.discuss: What is our trigger level on the Anilao gauge, and who sounds the warning?

opts.t: Activate the flash-flood contingency plan: raise the EOC to Blue, warn the riverside BDRRMCs by radio, siren and bell, start pre-emptive evacuation of riverbank households now, and pre-position WASAR teams on high ground.
opts.why: Short-lead hazards need city-level early action under the LGU's own authority. Multiple warning channels reach people without phones; evacuation starts while it is still light.

opts.t: Request a State of Imminent Disaster from RDRRMC 8 before ordering any evacuation.
opts.why: The RA 12287 declaration works on a 3-day lead time; you have three hours. The IRR lets the city act early on its own discretion. Waiting for an unsuitable process wastes the only window you have.

opts.t: Wait for PAGASA to raise a Red warning to be sure.
opts.why: The river gauge is the better trigger here; by the time Red is raised, lead time may be under an hour.

opts.t: Post an advisory on the City Facebook page and let families decide.
opts.why: One channel and no instruction. At night, with power at risk, sirens, radios and BDRRMC house-to-house warnings reach far more people.

phases.name: Overtopping
situation: The Anilao has overtopped near the bridge. Water is chest-deep in parts of West and rising. 71 rescue requests: families on rooftops, an elderly couple trapped, a jeepney stalled in the current.
Volunteers with private bancas are heading into the water. A crowd is gathering on the bridge to watch.
phases.intel: SOFR: current is too strong for paddled bancas. Only WASAR-trained teams with PFDs and throw lines should enter. The bridge approach is unstable.
phases.hint: Who goes into moving water, and who keeps the bridge clear?
phases.discuss: How do we use willing volunteers safely?

opts.t: Establish an ICP on high ground; Operations assigns WASAR teams by sector with PFDs and throw lines; the Safety Officer stops untrained volunteers from entering the current and reassigns them to EC support; PNP clears the bridge.
opts.why: Only trained, equipped teams enter moving water. Volunteers are redirected, not wasted, and the bridge closure prevents secondary casualties.

opts.t: Let the volunteers go; every boat helps.
opts.why: Untrained rescuers in swift water become victims. Self-deployment also breaks accountability (no check-in, ICS 211).

fx.e: Volunteer banca capsized: 3 rescuers in the water

opts.t: Pull all teams back until the water recedes.
opts.why: WASAR teams exist for this. With the right equipment and sector assignments they can work safely now.

opts.t: Send all teams to the stalled jeepney first; it is on the news.
opts.why: Media attention is not a triage criterion. Assign teams by life threat across all sectors.

phases.name: Missing persons
situation: Water is falling slowly. Barangays report 17 people missing, but names repeat across lists. Two bodies have been recovered near the river mouth.
A local page has posted a "death toll of 40". Families are arriving at the EOC asking for news.
phases.intel: Planning: after de-duplication the 17 reports are 11 unique names. PNP SOCO is available for identification. The MDM cluster is DILG-led; the CHO can support.
phases.hint: One list, one voice.
phases.discuss: Who owns the missing-persons list, and who may release figures?

opts.t: Planning keeps a single, de-duplicated missing-persons list; open a family assistance desk with CSWDO; follow MDM procedures with PNP SOCO for identification; the PIO releases only verified figures and corrects the rumor.
opts.why: Follows NDRRMC MC No. 19, s. 2016 on the dead and missing; one verified list and one public voice protect families and credibility.

opts.t: Confirm the "40" figure for now; correct it later if needed.
opts.why: Releasing an unverified death toll harms families and the city's credibility.

opts.t: Let each barangay release its own list to save time.
opts.why: Overlapping lists inflate numbers and confuse families. Lists are consolidated by Planning.

opts.t: Say nothing until all missing persons are found.
opts.why: Silence fuels rumors. Give regular verified updates even when the count is incomplete.

phases.name: Recovery & health
situation: Water has receded. Mud and debris fill West and East. Many residents waded through floodwater for hours.
1,900 families remain in ECs, most in schools. Classes are due to resume.
phases.intel: CHO: residents who waded in floodwater are at risk of leptospirosis; the DOH protocol covers prophylaxis for exposed persons. CENRO notes watershed cover upstream has declined.
phases.hint: Think health, shelter and the root cause.
phases.discuss: Which lesson from 1991 and from tonight goes into the LDRRMP?

opts.t: CHO runs leptospirosis advisories and prophylaxis per the DOH protocol; WASH and debris clearing by area; move families out of school ECs into planned alternative shelter; RDANA; schedule an AAR that feeds watershed actions (CENRO) into the LDRRMP.
opts.why: Covers the main post-flood health risk, protects education, and closes the loop to mitigation — the "M" in DDRiVE-M.

opts.t: Start classes tomorrow; families can return home.
opts.why: Many houses are not habitable. Moving families out needs a destination and a health check.

opts.t: Keep all ECs open indefinitely while waiting for national help.
opts.why: Recovery is led locally. Plan transitional shelter and request specific support through the proper channel.

opts.t: Focus only on debris clearing; health will take care of itself.
opts.why: Post-flood leptospirosis is a known, preventable risk. Leaving it out costs lives.

SCENARIOS.name: Leyte earthquake
SCENARIOS.lead: CDRRMO (IC); BFP and City Engineering in unified command on fire/structure sites
SCENARIOS.blurb: A shallow magnitude 6.5 earthquake on the Leyte segment of the Philippine Fault. PEIS VII in Ormoc. A commercial building partly collapses in Barangay South.
SCENARIOS.context: Western Leyte sits along the Philippine Fault Zone. In July 2017 a magnitude 6.5 earthquake struck Ormoc and nearby towns, affecting 10,167 families in the city (CDRA, citing DSWD DROMIC). Critical facilities to check first: hospitals, bridges over the Anilao and Malbasag, the port, schools and the Tongonan geothermal area.

phases.name: First minutes

warn.t: PHIVOLCS: M6.5 · PEIS VII in Ormoc

situation: Strong shaking lasted about 20 seconds. PHIVOLCS reports magnitude 6.5, depth 10 km, PEIS VII in Ormoc. Aftershocks continue.
Calls report cracked walls at a hospital, a partly collapsed building in South and fires in two houses. People are running toward the bay.
phases.intel: PHIVOLCS bulletin: the epicenter is onshore. Check the bulletin for any tsunami information rather than guessing. The geothermal operator reports wells shut in safely.
phases.hint: Where does tsunami information come from?
phases.discuss: Which facilities do we check in the first hour, and who checks them?

opts.t: Raise the EOC to Red; the Mayor delegates authority to the IC; send rapid assessment teams to hospitals, bridges, the port and schools; the PIO relays the official PHIVOLCS tsunami information and tells people to stay away from damaged buildings.
opts.why: Activates command fast, checks critical facilities first, and uses PHIVOLCS as the only source on tsunami threat, stopping a panic move in the wrong direction.

opts.t: Order everyone to the coast and open ground by the bay to escape falling buildings.
opts.why: Sending people to the shore after strong shaking is dangerous until PHIVOLCS rules out a tsunami.

fx.e: Crowd crush at the port gate

opts.t: Wait for the PHIVOLCS final report before activating anything.
opts.why: Activation follows the felt intensity and reported damage, not the final report.

opts.t: Send every responder to the collapsed building immediately.
opts.why: Converging on one site leaves hospitals and bridges unchecked. Assess first, then assign.

phases.name: Collapsed structure
situation: At the partly collapsed three-storey building in South, an estimated eight people are trapped. BFP is fighting a small fire next door. Bystanders are pulling at debris.
26 injured people are sitting at the roadside; ambulances are arriving from three directions.
phases.intel: City Engineering: the north wall is leaning; another aftershock could bring it down. Two USAR-trained teams are available. The nearest hospital has limited surge capacity.
phases.hint: Two agencies with jurisdiction, one site. Who commands, and who enters?
phases.discuss: When do we let rescuers enter a damaged structure?

opts.t: Form a unified command (CDRRMO, BFP, City Engineering) at an ICP upwind; cordon the site; no entry until the engineer marks safe zones; USAR teams go in with shoring; set up a casualty collection point with START triage and distribute patients across hospitals.
opts.why: Unified command fits multi-agency sites; structural assessment protects rescuers; START triage and patient distribution follow MCI practice (DOH AO No. 155, s. 2004).

opts.t: Let bystanders and responders keep digging; speed matters.
opts.why: Uncontrolled digging can bring the structure down on victims and rescuers. The Safety Officer stops it.

opts.t: Send all 26 injured to the nearest hospital.
opts.why: One hospital is overwhelmed while others sit empty. Triage and distribute.

opts.t: BFP takes sole command since there is a fire.
opts.why: The fire is one part of a structural rescue and MCI. Agencies with jurisdiction share command.

phases.name: Second operational period
situation: Six of the eight trapped were rescued overnight. A landslide blocks the road to upland barangays; one barangay has had no contact since the quake.
Responders have worked 16 hours. Offers of help are arriving from neighbouring LGUs and private companies.
phases.intel: Logistics: two excavators are available but no fuel plan. Liaison: three LGUs and two companies want to send teams. A barangay runner says the isolated barangay has injured residents.
phases.hint: Who rests, who replaces them, and how do offers become assignments?
phases.discuss: How do we take offers of help without losing control?

opts.t: Run the planning meeting: an IAP for this operational period with relief shifts for tired crews; send a team on foot or by motorbike to the isolated barangay; Liaison routes offers through the EOC to check-in (ICS 211) and assignment; Logistics sets fuel and supply plans for the excavators.
opts.why: The planning cycle turns chaos into an IAP; crew rest protects capacity; check-in keeps every resource accountable.

opts.t: Accept every offer and tell teams to go wherever they see damage.
opts.why: Self-deployed teams are untracked and unsafe, and they duplicate effort.

opts.t: Keep the same crews working until all rescues are done.
opts.why: Fatigue causes injuries and errors. Plan relief shifts.

opts.t: Wait for the road to be cleared before contacting the isolated barangay.
opts.why: Silence from a barangay is a priority signal. Reach it by any available means.

phases.name: Re-entry & recovery
situation: Search and rescue is complete. 2,100 families are in tents or ECs; many are afraid to go home. Owners want to reopen shops in South.
Schools have visible cracks.
phases.intel: OBO can inspect about 120 buildings a day with current staff. DepEd needs a safety certification before reopening schools. CHO reports many residents with anxiety and poor sleep.
phases.hint: Who certifies that a building is safe?
phases.discuss: How do we prioritize building inspections?

opts.t: OBO inspects and tags buildings (inspected / restricted / unsafe), schools and hospitals first; families return only to inspected houses; set up MHPSS with the CHO; RDANA feeds the CDRRMC's recommendation on a state of calamity; plan demobilization and the AAR.
opts.why: Re-entry based on inspection prevents deaths in aftershocks. MHPSS and RDANA cover needs, and evidence supports any declaration.

opts.t: Let owners reopen shops if they feel it is safe.
opts.why: Owners are not structural assessors; aftershocks can collapse damaged buildings.

opts.t: Keep everyone out of the city proper for two weeks.
opts.why: Blanket closure stalls recovery. Use inspection tags to reopen safe areas.

opts.t: Reopen schools once classes are scheduled.
opts.why: Schools need certification first.

SCENARIOS.name: Ormoc port vessel capsizing
SCENARIOS.blurb: A passenger motorbanca bound for the Camotes Islands capsizes just outside Ormoc port in a squall. About 150 aboard; the manifest does not match the count.
SCENARIOS.context: Ormoc port links Leyte to Cebu and the Camotes Islands. In July 2015 a passenger motorbanca capsized near the port, with dozens dead. The PCG leads maritime search and rescue; the city runs the shoreside response: casualty collection, hospitals, families and information.

phases.name: Capsizing
situation: A motorbanca capsized 400 m from the port breakwater at 12:15H. Fishermen and port workers are already pulling people from the water.
PCG Station Ormoc has launched two boats. The EOC asks who is in charge.
phases.intel: PCG has jurisdiction over maritime SAR. The port has space for a casualty collection point near the terminal. Hospitals have not yet been alerted.
phases.hint: Whose jurisdiction is the water? Whose is the shore?
phases.discuss: Where does the PCG's command end and the city's begin?

opts.t: Establish unified command: PCG leads at sea, CDRRMO leads shoreside. Set up a casualty collection point at the port, alert all hospitals for an MCI, PNP secures the terminal, and the EOC rises to Red.
opts.why: Respects PCG's maritime mandate while the city runs what it is responsible for, under one set of objectives.

opts.t: CDRRMO takes command of everything, including the boats.
opts.why: The city does not have maritime SAR jurisdiction or assets. Taking over the sea creates conflict, not speed.

opts.t: Leave it to the PCG; it is a maritime incident.
opts.why: Survivors, casualties and families come ashore in the city. Without a shoreside command, triage and transport fail.

opts.t: Ask private boats to stop rescuing until the PCG arrives.
opts.why: Bystanders are already saving lives in calm water near shore. Coordinate them; do not stop them.

phases.name: Mass casualties
situation: 96 people have been rescued; 31 are at the shore casualty collection point, several unconscious after near-drowning. Ambulances are lining up at the terminal gate.
Relatives are pushing into the area.
phases.intel: Hospitals report: two can take about 20 patients each; the nearest has 8 beds free. DOH-Eastern Visayas can activate surge support.
phases.hint: Sort, then spread.
phases.discuss: Who decides which hospital each patient goes to?

opts.t: Run START triage at the casualty point; a transport officer assigns patients to hospitals by capacity; one-way ambulance lanes; PNP cordons the area and directs families to a separate family assistance desk.
opts.why: MCI practice: triage, then distribute by capacity so no hospital is overwhelmed. Separating families keeps the treatment area clear.

opts.t: Send everyone to the nearest hospital as fast as possible.
opts.why: The nearest hospital would receive far more patients than it can treat.

opts.t: Treat everyone at the port until doctors arrive.
opts.why: Critical near-drowning cases need hospital care; triage and transport.

opts.t: Let relatives take survivors home or to hospital themselves.
opts.why: Untracked departures make the missing count wrong and survivors may not be checked.

phases.name: Missing & families
situation: The manifest lists 132 names; rescuers count 118 survivors and 9 dead; witnesses say there were children not on the manifest.
TV crews ask for the names of the dead. Families are at the port.
phases.intel: Planning has three different counts. CSWDO can staff the family desk. PCG will continue search at sea overnight.
phases.hint: Who reconciles the numbers, and who is told first?
phases.discuss: How do we inform families before the public?

opts.t: Planning reconciles the manifest, survivor list and hospital lists into one count; CSWDO runs the family desk with MHPSS; next of kin are informed before any name is released; the PIO gives scheduled briefings with verified numbers, coordinated with the PCG.
opts.why: One reconciled list, families informed first, and joint information with the PCG.

opts.t: Release the manifest names now so families know.
opts.why: Releasing unverified names causes false hope or false grief; the manifest is known to be wrong.

opts.t: Let the PCG and the city brief media separately.
opts.why: Two voices give two numbers. Joint information under unified command.

opts.t: Close the port to families until search ends.
opts.why: Families need a place, information and support. A desk with clear updates works better than a closed gate.

phases.name: Retrieval & transition
situation: Search has moved to retrieval. Four people remain missing. MARINA and the PCG have opened an investigation.
Media ask the city whether the boat was overloaded.
phases.intel: Liaison: MARINA and PCG lead the investigation. Relatives need help with documents and claims.
phases.hint: What is the city's role in an investigation it does not lead?
phases.discuss: What will we change in the port contingency plan?

opts.t: Support PCG retrieval; refer cause questions to MARINA and PCG; continue family support, documents and MHPSS; demobilize city resources in order; hold an AAR and update the port contingency plan with PCG.
opts.why: Stays within the city's mandate, supports families, and turns lessons into plan updates.

opts.t: Tell media the boat was clearly overloaded.
opts.why: Speculation can prejudice an investigation led by other agencies.

opts.t: Withdraw all city support since rescue is over.
opts.why: Families still need support during retrieval.

opts.t: Keep all response resources at the port until the investigation ends.
opts.why: Demobilize what is no longer needed; keep only what retrieval and family support need.

SCENARIOS.name: Tongonan geothermal gas release
SCENARIOS.lead: Unified command: BFP (hazmat) + CDRRMO + facility emergency team
SCENARIOS.blurb: A ruptured pipeline at the Tongonan geothermal field releases hydrogen sulfide (H2S). Residents nearby report a rotten-egg smell, then dizziness.
SCENARIOS.context: Barangay Tongonan in upland Ormoc hosts the Mahanagdong A and Malitbog geothermal plants (CDRA critical facilities); the PNOC access roads there are rated high risk for landslides. H2S is heavier than air and collects in low ground and valleys; at high levels it deadens the sense of smell, so "the smell is gone" is not a safety signal. The facility operator has its own emergency team and monitoring equipment.

phases.name: First report
situation: The facility operator reports a pipeline rupture and says its team is isolating the line. Residents in two sitios downslope call the barangay about a strong smell; five report dizziness.
Wind is light, flowing downslope toward the houses.
phases.intel: Operator: monitors near the fence show H2S above safe limits. BFP's hazmat team is 50 minutes away. H2S collects in low ground.
phases.hint: Distance, direction and elevation.
phases.discuss: What does the facility's emergency plan say we should do?

opts.t: Form a unified command with BFP and the operator's emergency team; set an exclusion zone; evacuate the downslope sitios crosswind and uphill, away from low ground; no entry without SCBA; alert the CHO and hospitals; raise the EOC to Blue.
opts.why: Treats H2S correctly (heavier than air, follows low ground), keeps unprotected responders out, and puts agencies with jurisdiction and expertise in one command.

opts.t: Send the barangay tanod to check on the dizzy residents.
opts.why: Untrained, unprotected responders entering an H2S area become casualties.

opts.t: Tell residents to stay indoors with windows closed until the leak stops.
opts.why: Sheltering in houses in a low area where gas pools is risky at these levels. Evacuate crosswind and uphill.

opts.t: Let the operator handle it; it is their facility.
opts.why: Residents outside the fence are the city's responsibility. Use a unified command.

phases.name: Wind shift
situation: The wind has shifted. Readings are rising near an elementary school in a hollow 1.2 km away, where classes have just started.
Parents are driving toward the school.
phases.intel: The school's planned evacuation route runs down into the valley. An uphill route is available on foot.
phases.hint: Which way is safe for gas that sinks?
phases.discuss: How do we reunite children and parents safely?

opts.t: Evacuate the school by the uphill route on foot; PNP holds parents' vehicles at a reunification point outside the zone; the PIO issues one clear advisory naming the zone; expand the exclusion zone.
opts.why: Uphill, crosswind movement avoids pooled gas; a reunification point prevents a traffic jam in the danger zone.

opts.t: Use the school's planned evacuation route down the valley.
opts.why: The planned route leads into the area where H2S collects.

opts.t: Keep the children inside the school.
opts.why: The school is in a hollow where gas will accumulate.

opts.t: Let parents collect their children directly.
opts.why: Cars converging in the zone block responders and expose parents.

phases.name: Exposure care
situation: The operator has isolated the line; readings are falling. 23 people have symptoms; 4 were briefly unconscious.
Social media claims the river is "poisoned".
phases.intel: CHO: people briefly unconscious from H2S need hospital evaluation. EMB can test water and air. The operator has monitoring data.
phases.hint: Treat, verify, then speak.
phases.discuss: Who confirms water and air are safe?

opts.t: Send the 4 who lost consciousness to hospital and assess the others at a medical post; request EMB sampling; the PIO answers the river rumor with what is known and when test results will come.
opts.why: Medical priority by severity, independent verification, and honest communication that says what is not yet known.

opts.t: Announce that the river is safe.
opts.why: No test has been done. Claims without evidence damage trust when corrected.

opts.t: Discharge everyone since readings are falling.
opts.why: Victims who lost consciousness need evaluation.

opts.t: Avoid comment until EMB results come in.
opts.why: Silence lets the rumor run.

phases.name: Re-entry
situation: Readings are near background. Residents want to go home to their animals and crops. The operator wants to restart the line.
phases.intel: Restart of the line is the operator's decision under its regulators. Re-entry of residents is the city's decision.
phases.hint: Who decides each thing?
phases.discuss: What goes into a joint LGU–facility contingency plan?

opts.t: Allow phased re-entry after joint monitoring by the operator and EMB confirms safe levels, starting with higher ground; hold a community meeting; demobilize; schedule an AAR to update the joint LGU–facility contingency plan.
opts.why: Evidence-based, phased re-entry and a joint plan update.

opts.t: Let residents return now; the smell is gone.
opts.why: Loss of smell is not a reliable safety sign for H2S.

opts.t: Keep the area closed until the line is restarted.
opts.why: Re-entry depends on monitoring, not the restart.

opts.t: Let the operator decide on re-entry for residents.
opts.why: Residents' safety outside the fence is a city decision.

SCENARIOS.name: Upland rain-induced landslide
SCENARIOS.lead: CDRRMO (IC) with City Engineering, BFP, PNP and BDRRMCs
SCENARIOS.blurb: Days of shear-line rain saturate the slopes of upland Ormoc. Cracks open above a sitio; then a slope fails and cuts the road.
SCENARIOS.context: The CDRA names Patag, Don Carlos B. Rivilla Sr., Sumangga, Ipil and Hibunawon as most exposed to rain-induced landslides, and rates the PNOC roads, Margen Road 3 and the Lake Danao Circumferential Road as high-risk lifelines. RA 12287 covers rain-induced landslides, but warning lead times are usually short, so community-based early warning and the City's own discretion carry the decision.

phases.name: Warning signs

warn.t: Orange rainfall warning · MGB landslide threat advisory

situation: A third day of rain. PAGASA has an Orange warning over western Leyte and the MGB advisory lists upland Ormoc barangays as susceptible to landslides.
BDRRMC observers in a sitio of Patag report new tension cracks above 40 houses and muddy springs on the slope. The road below is the only way out.
phases.intel: City Engineering: the cracks match the CDRA high-susceptibility zone. Heavy equipment is at the city yard, two hours away. The barangay has a covered court on stable ground.
phases.hint: Signs on the slope are the trigger. Who moves first, and where does equipment wait?
phases.discuss: What are our landslide early-warning signs, and who calls the evacuation?

opts.t: Raise the EOC to Blue; on CDRRMO's recommendation the Mayor orders pre-emptive evacuation of households below the cracks to the covered court; close the road to traffic; pre-position heavy equipment and a rescue team at a safe staging point away from the slope toe.
opts.why: Community warning signs justify early action under the City's own discretion (RA 12287 IRR, Rule IV, Sec. 1). Equipment waits off the runout path.

opts.t: Send a team up the slope to measure the cracks before deciding.
opts.why: Assessment helps, but people below a failing slope should move first. Measure from a safe position after evacuation.

opts.t: Wait for the MGB to confirm in writing.
opts.why: Slopes can fail in hours. A written confirmation is not a precondition for pre-emptive evacuation.

fx.c: Slope fails with families still in place

opts.t: Bring the excavator in now to cut a drainage channel across the slope.
opts.why: Heavy equipment on a saturated, cracking slope can trigger the failure and put operators in the runout path.

phases.name: Slope failure
situation: The slope failed at 22:20H. Four houses that had not evacuated are buried; seven people are reported missing. Debris has cut the road in two places.
Neighbours are digging with shovels in the dark. Rain continues.
phases.intel: City Engineering: the scarp is still moving; a secondary slide is likely while rain continues. A geologist can reach the site at first light.
phases.hint: Unstable ground, darkness, rain. Who enters, and who watches the slope?
phases.discuss: When do we stop rescue on an unstable slope?

opts.t: Set the ICP at a safe distance; cordon the debris; post slope spotters with a clear evacuation signal; trained SRR teams work only in zones the engineer marks safe; record missing persons through Planning; request a geologist and lighting through the EOC.
opts.why: Spotters and safe zones protect rescuers from a second slide; a single missing-persons list starts the MDM process.

opts.t: Let neighbours keep digging; every minute counts.
opts.why: Untrained diggers on a moving slope risk becoming victims of a secondary slide.

opts.t: Bring in the excavator to dig fast.
opts.why: Machinery on unstable debris can trigger collapse and harm buried survivors.

opts.t: Suspend all work until the geologist arrives at dawn.
opts.why: Some work can continue safely with spotters in marked zones; a full stop may cost lives.

phases.name: Isolated barangay
situation: Two missing persons were found alive overnight. The road will take three days to clear. About 600 residents beyond the slide are cut off; a sick child needs evacuation.
Offers of help arrive from neighbouring LGUs and a private company with a small helicopter.
phases.intel: Logistics: a foot trail is passable. RDRRMC 8 can request AFP air assets. Weather may allow flights after 10:00H.
phases.hint: Reach, resupply and request through the right channel.
phases.discuss: How do we decide between road, trail and air?

opts.t: Send a medical team and supplies by foot trail now; request air support through the EOC to RDRRMC 8 for the child and for resupply when weather allows; Liaison routes offers to check-in and assignment; keep spotters on the slide.
opts.why: Uses what works now, asks for air assets through the proper channel, and keeps every offer accountable (NDRRMC Memo No. 131: IMT requests go through the EOC).

opts.t: Tell the private helicopter to fly in whenever the pilot thinks it is safe.
opts.why: Untracked air operations without coordination are unsafe and duplicate effort.

opts.t: Wait until the road is cleared.
opts.why: Three days without access is not acceptable for a sick child and 600 residents.

opts.t: Send the excavator crew to dig through the slide now.
opts.why: Clearing must follow the geologist's assessment while the scarp is still moving.

phases.name: Re-entry and land use
situation: Rain has stopped. Families want to return to houses near the scarp. The barangay asks the City to rebuild the road along the same line.
phases.intel: The geologist has mapped the scarp and runout zone. The CLUP and zoning ordinance set rules for hazard zones; CSWDO can arrange transitional shelter.
phases.hint: Who decides whether a slope is safe to live on?
phases.discuss: What changes in the LDRRMP and zoning after this event?

opts.t: Keep households in the mapped runout zone out until a geohazard assessment clears them; arrange transitional shelter; RDANA; refer no-build and relocation recommendations to CPDO for the CLUP and zoning; schedule the AAR.
opts.why: Re-entry based on assessment, shelter for the displaced, and mitigation through land use — the "M" in DDRiVE-M.

opts.t: Let families return now that the rain has stopped.
opts.why: Saturated slopes can fail days after rain stops.

opts.t: Rebuild the road on the same alignment immediately.
opts.why: Rebuilding in the runout zone repeats the risk.

opts.t: Close the whole barangay indefinitely.
opts.why: Blanket closure ignores the mapped safe areas and stalls recovery.

ALERT_INFO.white: WHITE — normal operations. Operations Center monitors and reports under regular mandates. LGU report times: 06:00 and 18:00 (RDRRMC 8 Res. No. 12-006).
ALERT_INFO.blue: BLUE — heightened alert. At least 50% of human and material resources on standby for duty or deployment; triggered by detection, monitoring or PDRA results. EOC operated by directive; harmonized reporting starts. Reports at 09:00 and 19:00.
ALERT_INFO.red: RED — full alert. All human and material resources available for duty and deployment; response clusters and IMT may be activated; inter-cluster action planning. Reports at 09:00 and 19:00.

J: Management of the Dead and Missing

ro.name: Where the Mayor stands
situation: Typhoon response, day 1. The IC invites you to "join Unified Command" at the ICP, and TV crews are waiting there.
ro.intel: NDRRMC MC No. 4, s. 2012: the RO sets policy and priorities and delegates authority; the IC manages the scene.

opts.t: Stay as Responsible Official: confirm the delegation of authority in writing, set priorities and limits, receive briefings at the EOC, and visit the ICP briefly without directing tactics.
opts.why: Keeps the policy layer intact and the IC free to manage the incident.

opts.t: Join Unified Command at the ICP as a member.
opts.why: Unified Command is for agencies with jurisdiction at the scene. The Mayor delegates to the IC rather than sharing tactical command.

opts.t: Take over as IC for the visibility.
opts.why: It removes the policy layer and puts a non-specialist on tactics; designate a qualified IC.

opts.t: Direct rescue teams by phone from your car.
opts.why: Bypasses the chain of command and the accountability system.

ro.name: Ending operations
situation: Day 4. The IC recommends terminating search and rescue: all reports are cleared and teams are tired. Some councillors want operations to continue "to show presence".
ro.intel: NDRRMC Memo No. 131, s. 2018: the IC recommends termination; the RO approves based on situation updates.

opts.t: Approve termination on the IC's recommendation after a situation update, with a demobilization plan and a shift to early recovery.
opts.why: Follows the Memo 131 sequence and moves resources to where they are now needed.

opts.t: Keep operations running for another week for public confidence.
opts.why: Holding resources without a task wastes capacity and tires responders.

opts.t: Order termination yourself without consulting the IC.
opts.why: The IC has the ground picture; the RO approves on that basis.

opts.t: Let each agency leave when it decides to.
opts.why: Uncoordinated withdrawal leaves gaps and untracked resources.

ro.name: State of calamity
situation: Barangay captains ask you to declare a state of calamity today by Executive Order so they can use their funds.
ro.intel: RA 10121 Sec. 16: the Sanggunian declares on the recommendation of the LDRRMC, based on assessment results.
ro.hint: Which body declares, on whose recommendation?

opts.t: Convene the CDRRMC to review RDANA results; if criteria are met, the CDRRMC recommends to the Sangguniang Panlungsod, which declares by resolution.
opts.why: Correct body and evidence base; the resolution is also what RDRRMC 8 needs before reporting the declaration.

opts.t: Sign an EO declaring a state of calamity now.
opts.why: A state of calamity is declared by the Sanggunian, not by the Mayor's EO.

opts.t: Tell barangays to declare their own states of calamity.
opts.why: Each declaration follows its own council process; coordinate rather than delegate the decision.

opts.t: Wait for the President to declare one.
opts.why: Local declarations do not wait for a national one.

eoc.name: A resource request
situation: The IC radios the EOC: "Need two more rescue boats in the West sector within the hour."
eoc.intel: NDRRMC Memo No. 131, s. 2018: all IMT resource requests go to the EOC; the EOC coordinates with the response clusters to fill them.
eoc.hint: Resource employer, resource provider — who sits between?

opts.t: Log the request, source the boats through the clusters and partner agencies, track them to delivery and confirm arrival with the IC.
opts.why: The EOC is the link between the IMT and the clusters, and tracks the request to completion.

opts.t: Tell the IC to call the PCG directly.
opts.why: Direct calls bypass tracking and create duplicate requests.

opts.t: Send EOC staff to the West sector to run the boats.
opts.why: The EOC coordinates; it does not take tactical command.

opts.t: Wait for the next coordination meeting.
opts.why: Urgent requests are processed as they arrive.

eoc.name: Where to put the ICP
situation: The IC proposes running the ICP from the EOC building "so everyone is in one room".
eoc.intel: NDRRMC Memo No. 131, s. 2018, item 9.2.5.3: the EOC and ICP shall not be co-located.
eoc.hint: Coordination and command in the same room?

opts.t: Keep the ICP on scene at a safe, accessible location; link it to the EOC by radio and a liaison; the EOC stays the coordination hub.
opts.why: Follows Memo 131 and keeps command close to the incident.

opts.t: Agree; one room is simpler.
opts.why: Co-location blurs command and coordination and takes the IC away from the scene.

opts.t: Move the EOC to the ICP instead.
opts.why: The EOC must stay at a safe, hazard-free site with its equipment and links.

opts.t: Run without an ICP; the EOC can direct teams.
opts.why: Without on-scene command, tactics are directed by people who cannot see the scene.

eoc.name: First report under Red alert
situation: A flash flood hit at 19:30H. RDRRMC 8 is asking for numbers; barangay figures are arriving by text and do not agree.
eoc.intel: RDRRMOC SOPG: initial report within 2 hours to confirm the incident. RDRRMC 8 Res. 12-006: under Blue or Red alert, LGU reports are due by 09:00 and 19:00 on the harmonized template.

opts.t: Send an initial report within 2 hours (what, when, where, initial actions), then harmonized reports by 09:00 and 19:00 using Forms D–H, with figures validated before release.
opts.why: Meets the 2-hour initial report and the harmonized schedule with validated data.

opts.t: Forward the barangay texts as they arrive.
opts.why: Unvalidated, conflicting figures create confusion up the line.

opts.t: Report only when all figures are complete.
opts.why: The initial report confirms the event; completeness comes in later reports.

opts.t: Wait for RDRRMC 8 to call again.
opts.why: Reporting is a standing duty under Blue and Red alert.

ic.name: Setting up the ICP
situation: Typhoon landfall in 6 hours. You need an Incident Command Post.
ic.intel: The ICP should be safe, accessible and close enough to the scene, and not in the EOC (Memo No. 131).

opts.t: Set the ICP at a safe, elevated, accessible site near the most exposed area, separate from the EOC, with backup power and radio links.
opts.why: A safe, functioning ICP comes first; resources follow once command is set.

opts.t: Deploy all rescue teams first and set up the ICP later.
opts.why: Without command, deployed teams are untracked.

opts.t: Run the incident from the EOC.
opts.why: The EOC coordinates; command belongs on scene.

opts.t: Put the ICP at the coastal plaza for visibility.
opts.why: The coast is in the surge zone.

ic.name: Sizing the IMT
situation: City-wide typhoon impact: rescue, evacuation, relief and road clearing are all running at once.
ic.intel: ICS is modular: activate only the positions you need, but keep span of control at 3 to 7.

opts.t: Activate Command Staff and all four sections, with divisions by area so each supervisor manages 3–7 units.
opts.why: Matches the incident's complexity and keeps span of control workable.

opts.t: Run Operations and Logistics only; planning can wait.
opts.why: Without Planning there is no IAP or resource tracking.

opts.t: Let each agency run its own operation.
opts.why: Leads to duplication, gaps and no accountability.

opts.t: Form ad-hoc teams as people arrive.
opts.why: Standard structure lets arriving staff slot in quickly.

ic.name: Transfer of command
situation: An OCD-deployed IMT arrives to augment. Its leader is more experienced and will take over as IC.
ic.intel: Transfer of command needs a face-to-face briefing (ICS 201), a set effective time and notification of all staff.

opts.t: Brief the incoming IC face to face with ICS 201, agree an effective time, notify the RO, EOC and staff, and record the transfer.
opts.why: An orderly transfer avoids two ICs and lost information.

opts.t: Hand over the radio and leave.
opts.why: Without a briefing, the new IC starts blind.

opts.t: Keep command and treat the new team as advisers.
opts.why: Augmentation was requested to strengthen management; use it.

opts.t: Split command: you keep Operations, they take the rest.
opts.why: Unity of command requires one IC or a formal Unified Command.

sofr.name: Rescuer in the water
situation: A WASAR rescuer is swept off a boat in the Anilao current. Nearby teams start toward him without orders.
sofr.intel: A designated Rapid Intervention Team and accountability check are standard for responder emergencies.
sofr.hint: Rescue the rescuer without making more victims.

opts.t: Activate the rapid intervention team: the nearest equipped WASAR unit responds, other teams in that sector hold, and you run a personnel accountability check.
opts.why: A controlled response to a responder emergency; untrained convergence causes more casualties.

opts.t: Let every nearby team go.
opts.why: Uncontrolled convergence in swift water multiplies victims.

opts.t: Pull all operations citywide until he is found.
opts.why: Only the affected sector needs to hold.

opts.t: Ask the IC to request outside teams first.
opts.why: Act now with the nearest qualified unit.

sofr.name: Night operations
situation: Flood rescue continues past midnight. Visibility is poor and teams want to split up to cover more houses.
sofr.intel: Night work needs lighting, buddy pairs and tighter accountability.

opts.t: Consolidate teams, keep buddy pairs, deploy lighting, mark hazards and limit tasks to life-threatening calls until daylight.
opts.why: Reduces exposure while keeping life-saving work going.

opts.t: Continue at the same pace with smaller teams.
opts.why: Smaller teams at night raise the risk of losing responders.

opts.t: Stop all field work until dawn.
opts.why: Life-threatening calls may still be handled safely.

opts.t: Leave it to each team leader.
opts.why: The Safety Officer sets the safety rules for the operational period.

sofr.name: Fatigue
situation: Some responders have worked 18 hours straight and insist they are fine.
sofr.intel: Fatigue causes errors and injuries; time records and relief shifts are part of the IAP.
sofr.hint: Willing is not the same as fit.

opts.t: Enforce rest using the time records, bring in relief personnel in phases, and put rest periods into the next IAP.
opts.why: Protects responders and keeps capacity for the next period.

opts.t: Let them continue as long as they are willing.
opts.why: Fatigued responders cause accidents.

opts.t: Order everyone to rest at once.
opts.why: Phased relief keeps operations running.

opts.t: Hand out coffee and energy drinks.
opts.why: Stimulants do not replace rest.

pio.name: A fake warning
situation: A doctored "PAGASA Signal No. 5 for Ormoc" graphic is spreading on social media. The real bulletin shows Signal No. 2.
pio.intel: Warnings must come from mandated agencies; the RA 12287 IRR requires inclusive, timely, coordinated advisories across all platforms.
pio.hint: Correct it fast, everywhere, in the local language.

opts.t: Issue a correction quoting the official PAGASA bulletin on all City channels, radio and barangay networks, in Cebuano/Waray and English, with the actions people should take now.
opts.why: Fast, sourced, multi-channel and actionable.

opts.t: Ignore it; people will check PAGASA themselves.
opts.why: Rumors spread faster than corrections; silence lets panic or complacency grow.

opts.t: Post a correction on the City page only.
opts.why: One channel misses people without data or power.

opts.t: Ask the platform to delete it and say nothing else.
opts.why: Takedowns are slow; the public needs the correct information now.

pio.name: Names of the dead
situation: Media ask for the names of three people found dead. Families have not all been told.
pio.intel: RDRRMC 8 template: "Dead (confirmed)" needs PNP identification or DVI processing; others are "for verification and validation".
pio.hint: Families before the public; confirmed before reported.

opts.t: Release counts in the correct categories (confirmed / for verification); release names only after next-of-kin notification and PNP confirmation.
opts.why: Protects families and the accuracy of official figures.

opts.t: Release the names now; it is public interest.
opts.why: Families learning of a death from the news causes harm, and errors are hard to undo.

opts.t: Refuse to give any figures.
opts.why: Verified counts can be shared; silence feeds speculation.

opts.t: Let the barangays release their own lists.
opts.why: Multiple sources give conflicting figures.

pio.name: Reaching everyone
situation: Pre-emptive evacuation is ordered. Upland GIDA sitios have no signal; some residents are deaf or blind.
pio.intel: The RA 12287 IRR requires advisories that consider GIDAs and are inclusive.
pio.hint: Which channels reach people without phones?

opts.t: Combine radio, sirens, barangay bells and house-to-house BDRRMC warnings, with visual signals and sign-language-ready messages, and confirm receipt from each barangay.
opts.why: Multiple channels and confirmation close the gaps.

opts.t: Send a text blast to all subscribers.
opts.why: Misses people without signal or phones.

opts.t: Post on social media and radio only.
opts.why: Misses people who cannot hear or have no power.

opts.t: Rely on the media to spread the word.
opts.why: The City is responsible for warning its residents.

lofr.name: Corporate offer
situation: A company offers 20 trucks and 50 employee volunteers and asks where to send them.
lofr.intel: The RA 12287 IRR provides for mobilizing ACDVs, CSOs and the private sector through a strategic deployment plan.

opts.t: Route the offer through the EOC: check in vehicles and volunteers, brief them, and assign low-risk tasks under supervision; record it for later recognition and cost tracking.
opts.why: Accountable use of private help without self-deployment.

opts.t: Tell them to go wherever they see need.
opts.why: Self-deployment duplicates effort and puts untrained people at risk.

opts.t: Decline for liability reasons.
opts.why: Supervised, low-risk tasks use the help safely.

opts.t: Accept and leave them unsupervised.
opts.why: Untracked volunteers create safety and liability problems.

lofr.name: Unannounced team
situation: A rescue team from a neighbouring LGU arrives at the ICP without prior coordination.
lofr.intel: All arriving resources check in (ICS 211) before assignment.
lofr.hint: First stop for any arriving resource.

opts.t: Direct them to check-in, brief them on local conditions and safety, and pass them to Operations for assignment.
opts.why: Integrates help while keeping accountability.

opts.t: Send them straight to the hardest-hit area.
opts.why: Skipping check-in leaves them untracked.

opts.t: Send them home; they did not coordinate.
opts.why: Use available capacity after proper check-in.

opts.t: Let them work on their own.
opts.why: Freelancing teams risk duplication and responder safety.

lofr.name: Who leads?
situation: At a fire in a collapsed building, BFP and CDRRMO staff argue about who is in charge.
lofr.intel: Where more than one agency has jurisdiction, Unified Command sets one set of objectives.

opts.t: Bring both agency leads together to form Unified Command with one set of objectives and one IAP; you keep the agency contact list and resolve issues.
opts.why: Unified Command fits multi-jurisdiction incidents.

opts.t: Let the larger agency take over.
opts.why: Size does not settle jurisdiction.

opts.t: Let both run separate operations.
opts.why: Parallel commands at one site are unsafe.

opts.t: Ask the Mayor to decide on the phone.
opts.why: The RO sets policy; on-scene arrangements are settled through Unified Command.

osc.name: Organizing the field
situation: Rescue requests are coming from 12 barangays at once.
osc.intel: Divisions by area keep span of control at 3 to 7.

opts.t: Create geographic divisions with a supervisor each and assign teams by priority within each division.
opts.why: Keeps supervision workable and coverage balanced.

opts.t: Send one team to each barangay on its own.
opts.why: Unsupervised teams cannot be re-tasked or tracked well.

opts.t: Put everything into the worst-hit barangay.
opts.why: Leaves other life-threatening calls unanswered.

opts.t: Wait for complete damage reports.
opts.why: Life safety cannot wait for complete data.

osc.name: One boat, two divisions
situation: Two division supervisors both want the only swift-water boat.
osc.intel: Priorities: life safety, incident stabilization, property; the IAP sets objectives.

opts.t: Assign the boat to the division with the higher life threat under the IAP, and give the other an alternative or the next available asset.
opts.why: Resolves the conflict at the right level by need.

opts.t: Alternate it between divisions every hour.
opts.why: Equal shares ignore who is in danger.

opts.t: Let the supervisors decide between themselves.
opts.why: Operations resolves tactical conflicts.

opts.t: Escalate every such conflict to the IC.
opts.why: The OSC owns tactical allocation.

osc.name: Rising water at an EC
situation: Water is rising around an evacuation center holding 300 families.
osc.intel: Staged evacuation with assembly points and mixed transport prevents crowding.

opts.t: Run a staged evacuation to a safer EC with assembly points, vulnerable groups first, and trucks, boats and buses as available.
opts.why: Orderly and prioritized movement.

opts.t: Tell everyone to move to the second floor.
opts.why: Short-term only if water keeps rising.

opts.t: Request every bus in the city at once.
opts.why: Without staging, vehicles jam the route.

opts.t: Wait for the water to stabilize.
opts.why: Rising water around an EC needs action now.

psc.name: One picture
situation: CSWDO, BFP and CDRRMO each keep their own situation map with different figures.
psc.intel: A single Situation Unit and common operating picture prevent conflicting decisions.

opts.t: Set up one Situation Unit with a common map (GeoRiskPH layers plus field data) and one verified SitRep cycle on the harmonized template.
opts.why: One verified picture for all sections and agencies.

opts.t: Let each agency keep its own displays.
opts.why: Conflicting figures lead to conflicting decisions.

opts.t: Adopt whichever agency has the best software.
opts.why: The issue is a single verified process, not software.

opts.t: Use paper maps only.
opts.why: Paper is a good backup but not the whole system.

psc.name: A missed check-in
situation: Two field teams have missed their scheduled radio check-in by 40 minutes.
psc.intel: Resource accountability is a core ICS function.

opts.t: Verify their status with Operations at once, update resource tracking and alert the Safety Officer if contact cannot be made.
opts.why: Fast verification may save a team in trouble.

opts.t: Assume they are busy.
opts.why: Missed check-ins can mean an emergency.

opts.t: Report them to the IC as casualties.
opts.why: Premature; verify first.

opts.t: Wait for the next scheduled check-in.
opts.why: Too passive.

psc.name: A second storm
situation: While response continues, PAGASA tracks a second tropical cyclone that may affect Leyte in 4 days.
psc.intel: Planning looks ahead: PDRA for the new threat and contingency for the IAP.
psc.hint: Plan for the next period and the next hazard.

opts.t: Brief the IC, start a PDRA for the new threat, prepare an alternate IAP and check whether RA 12287 options apply within its window.
opts.why: Proactive planning for compounding hazards.

opts.t: Deal with it when it arrives.
opts.why: Reactive planning loses the lead time.

opts.t: Recommend full demobilization now.
opts.why: Current needs still exist.

opts.t: Tell the media first.
opts.why: Public information follows the plan, through the PIO.

lsc.name: Relief shortage
situation: Two ECs report food packs will run out tonight.
lsc.intel: CSWDO and the DSWD-led FNI cluster supply relief; requests go through the EOC.

opts.t: Activate the Supply Unit, request family food packs through the EOC from CSWDO and the FNI cluster, and set distribution points with tracking.
opts.why: Uses the established supply chain with accountability.

opts.t: Buy from the nearest stores with cash.
opts.why: Purchases must follow procurement rules and coordination.

opts.t: Wait for national relief.
opts.why: Local stocks and the cluster move first.

opts.t: Ask evacuees to share what they brought.
opts.why: The government must provide for evacuees.

lsc.name: Communications down
situation: Cell sites are down across the city; field teams are out of contact.
lsc.intel: ICS 205 radio plan; backup HF, ham and satellite links; the ETC cluster can support.

opts.t: Deploy portable repeaters, activate HF and amateur radio volunteers and the satellite phone, and update the ICS 205 communications plan.
opts.why: Restores links through planned redundancy.

opts.t: Wait for telcos to restore service.
opts.why: Responders cannot work blind for hours.

opts.t: Use motorcycle messengers only.
opts.why: Useful backup, not the main system.

opts.t: Pull teams back from areas without signal.
opts.why: Restore communications instead.

lsc.name: Flooded staging area
situation: The staging area at the city yard is flooding; vehicles and supplies are at risk.
lsc.intel: Staging can move independently of the ICP.

opts.t: Open an alternate staging area on higher ground, relocate in phases and inform Operations and the EOC of the new location.
opts.why: Keeps resources available without stopping operations.

opts.t: Send responders home until water recedes.
opts.why: Stops operations at the worst time.

opts.t: Have crews work from their vehicles.
opts.why: Temporary only.

opts.t: Move the whole ICP.
opts.why: Only staging needs to move.

fsc.name: Emergency purchase
situation: Operations needs 2,000 litres of fuel and generator parts today; normal bidding takes weeks.
fsc.intel: RA 12009 (which replaced RA 9184) keeps negotiated procurement for emergency cases; the HoPE confirms the grounds in writing.

opts.t: Use negotiated procurement for emergency cases under RA 12009 and its rules, with written justification from the HoPE and a full audit trail.
opts.why: Lawful speed with documentation that will pass audit.

opts.t: Run normal public bidding.
opts.why: Too slow for an emergency need.

opts.t: Pay from personal funds and claim later.
opts.why: Improper and unaccountable.

opts.t: Buy now and document later.
opts.why: Documentation must be done at the time.

fsc.name: Fund source for AA
situation: A State of Imminent Disaster is declared 4 days before landfall. Operations wants to spend the whole AA allocation today.
fsc.intel: RA 12287 IRR: beyond 3 days lead time, disbursement is capped at 30% of the AA allocation; within 3 days, up to 70%. AA comes from no more than 10% of the 70% LDRRMF; not the QRF.
fsc.hint: Which fund, and how much now?

opts.t: Charge AA to the AA line (no more than 10% of the 70% LDRRMF), release no more than 30% now, plan the rest for within 3 days, and track costs for the 45-day OCD report.
opts.why: Follows the IRR funding and tranche rules and prepares the report.

opts.t: Release the full allocation today.
opts.why: Exceeds the 30% cap for actions beyond 3 days.

opts.t: Use the Quick Response Fund.
opts.why: The QRF is not the AA source.

opts.t: Spend nothing until landfall.
opts.why: Defeats the purpose of anticipatory action.

fsc.name: Cost sharing
situation: Partner agencies and a neighbouring LGU are using equipment and fuel at the incident.
fsc.intel: Clear agreements and records avoid disputes later.

opts.t: Set cost-share agreements now, keep equipment-use and fuel logs, and prepare claims and reimbursements.
opts.why: Transparent records for all parties.

opts.t: Assume partners absorb their own costs.
opts.why: Unstated assumptions cause disputes.

opts.t: Bill everyone after the incident.
opts.why: Without records the bills cannot be supported.

opts.t: Track only City resources.
opts.why: Incomplete cost records.

LEARN.h:
ICS is the standard, on-scene, all-hazards incident management system adopted under NDRRMC MC No. 4, s. 2012 and reiterated in NDRRMC Memo No. 131, s. 2018. The IRR of RA 10121 (Rule 7) tasks the OCD to establish ICS as part of the country's on-scene response system.

Responsible Official (RO)

The City Mayor as Local Chief Executive and CDRRMC Chair. Sets policy, priorities and limits; delegates authority to the IC; approves termination on the IC's recommendation.

Incident Commander (IC)

Responsible for all incident activities: objectives, strategies, tactics, and requesting and releasing resources. Head of the IMT.

Command Staff

Public Information Officer, Safety Officer, Liaison Officer.

General Staff

Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Administration Section Chiefs.

Core principles: common terminology, modular organization, management by objectives, an Incident Action Plan for each operational period, manageable span of control (3–7), unity of command, unified command where jurisdictions overlap, accountability (check-in, ICS 211), and integrated communications (ICS 205).

Correction from the attached page: the Local Chief Executive is the Responsible Official, not the default Incident Commander. The RO designates a qualified IC.

Higher councils support the LGU, which remains the first responder. Requests for augmentation go from the City EOC to RDRRMC 8 / OCD Region VIII; national IMTs (NIMT) can be mobilized under NDRRMC Memo No. 44, s. 2016.

Activate or raise alert when

1 a natural or human-induced hazard threatens · 2 a planned event carries a threat · 3 an incident is ongoing · 4 a request for support needs multi-stakeholder coordination · 5 the RO directs.

Deactivate or downgrade when

1 the situation has improved · 2 tactical operations no longer need EOC support · 3 lower-level EOCs or agencies can manage · 4 the RO directs.

Five functions

Management · Operations (multi-stakeholder coordination) · Planning (information, SitReps, action planning) · Logistics (EOC facilities and support) · Finance/Admin.

Rules that matter on the day

The EOC links the clusters (resource providers) and the IMT (resource employer). All IMT resource requests go to the EOC. The EOC and ICP shall not be co-located. The IC recommends termination; the RO approves.

Response clusters

Alert levels in Eastern Visayas (RDRRMC 8 Res. No. 12-006; RDRRMOC SOPG): White normal monitoring · Blue heightened, at least 50% of resources on standby · Red full alert, all resources available. For slow-onset hazards the regional center also uses EPR protocols: Standby (green), ALPHA (yellow), BRAVO (orange), CHARLIE (red).

The Ten-Year Plan reports that Ormoc has a 24/7 EOC but that its operations still need a manual or SOP, and staff need ICS, EOC management and MDM training — the gap the MOO addresses.

Adopted by RDRRMC 8 Res. No. 12-006, s. 2023 and directed to all LDRRMCs, including the City LGOO of Ormoc, by DILG VIII on 26 Feb 2025. The template starts when the LGU raises a Blue alert or starts an emergency response.

When: White alert — by 06:00 and 18:00; Blue and Red — by 09:00 and 19:00 (LGU level). The regional center expects an initial report within 2 hours of an incident (RDRRMOC SOPG).

Categories that protect families: Dead (confirmed — identified by PNP or processed by DVI) vs Dead (for verification and validation); Missing (confirmed — with PNP report) vs Missing (for verification) vs Missing and found alive.

1. PDRA by the RDRRMC/LDRRMC shows "severe" projected impact for a forecastable hazard (severe winds, storm surge, floods, rain-induced landslides, lahar; drought).
  2. The CDRRMC coordinates with RDRRMC 8, which answers a local request within 24 hours. Nationally the NDRRMC recommends no later than 3 days before impact.
  3. The City Mayor declares the State of Imminent Disaster by Executive Order on RDRRMC recommendation.
  4. AA measures start at once: advisories, pre-positioning, pre-emptive evacuation and CCCM, ACDV and private-sector mobilization, FNI distribution, social amelioration (CBMS targeting), agri-fishery contingency, public health, education, transport, economy and environment measures.
  5. Lifted by the Mayor on RDRRMC recommendation when the hazard occurs (shift to response) or the forecast impact does not materialize. "No regrets": provisions still go to the intended beneficiaries.
  6. Report to OCD within 45 days of lifting: status of declarations, use of AA funds, economic and social costs minimized.

Money: no more than 10% of the 70% LDRRMF, plus the Special Trust Fund, donor funds, ODA and other lawful sources — not the QRF. Disbursement: at most 30% of the AA allocation for actions beyond 3 days lead time; up to 70% within 3 days.

Corrections from the attached pages: the IRR sets no fixed 30-day duration (the declaration runs to impact or non-occurrence); RA 12287 is the Declaration of State of Imminent Disaster Act, not a "DRRM enhancement" law; it does not open the QRF. Short-lead hazards such as Anilao–Malbasag flash floods still allow early action at the City's discretion (IRR Rule IV, Sec. 1). NDRRMC operational guidelines on triggers and DBM–COA funding guidelines are still pending.

People

About 241,692 residents and 56,208 households (2023 estimate, Ten-Year Plan); 85 barangays; 46,430 ha (CLUP).

Flood

46 barangays with critical flood risk, 59,545 people (Ten-Year Plan, from GeoRiskPH). 35 barangays flood every 1–3 years. Highest exposure: Punta, Liloan, Tambulilid (CDRA).

Storm surge

17.65% of the city's area susceptible. High risk: Naungan, Linao, Punta, Alegria, Batuan, Macabug (CDRA).

Landslide

Most exposed: Patag, Don Carlos B. Rivilla Sr., Sumangga, Ipil, Hibunawon. High-risk lifelines: PNOC roads, Margen Road 3, Lake Danao Circumferential Road (CDRA).

ICS courses referenced in the Gawad KALASAG assessment: ICS Executive Course, Basic ICS, Integrated Planning on ICS, and position courses; plus EOC management, RDANA and MDM. The Ten-Year Plan targets all levels of ICS training for City and barangay DRRMCs.

EOC readiness checklist (EOC Capability Assessment Checklist, 2017): staffing for at least 72 hours with a three-deep roster per position; an EOC operations manual; activation and deactivation conditions defined; generator tested at full load and fuel contracts; resource inventories kept current; a PSCP; an alternate EOC sited on the same criteria; location outside flood, landslide and hazmat zones; regular exercises with after-action reviews.

Exercise cycle for Ormoc: use this simulator for drills and tabletop exercises; record AAR findings as evidence for the "tested and improved" level in the Institutional Assessment Tool, and feed them into the MOO and the contingency plans.

The attached page proposed native iOS/macOS development; this web build runs on any device instead, including the EOC wall display.
